pointers.sentence: The subclass overrides `BaseSerializer.serialize` to return the text and a set of import lines, each a whole statement such as `"import datetime"`; `MigrationWriter.serialize` only calls `serializer_factory` and then that method (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:BaseSerializer`, `django/db/migrations/writer.py:MigrationWriter.serialize`).

The subclass overrides `BaseSerializer.serialize` to return the text and a set of import lines, each a whole statement such as `"import datetime"`; `MigrationWriter.serialize` only calls `serializer_factory` and then that method (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:BaseSerializer`, `django/db/migrations/writer.py:MigrationWriter.serialize`).
`serializer_factory` is a fixed sequence of tests, and the first a value passes decides (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:serializer_factory`).
What passes none of these reaches the registry, `Serializer._registry`: a dictionary from a type, or a tuple of types, to a serializer class (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:Serializer`).
`SET` returns a function, which the entry for functions would take, but sets a `deconstruct` on it, and the attribute is tested first (`django/db/models/deletion.py:SET`).

The **`deconstruct` protocol** is how an object says how to make it again: the method returns the dotted path of something to call, positional arguments and keyword arguments, and `DeconstructibleSerializer.serialize_deconstructed` writes the call (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:DeconstructibleSerializer.serialize_deconstructed`).

A path whose module is exactly `django.db.models` is written `models.` and the name, with `"from django.db import models"`; any other whole, with an import of its module (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:DeconstructibleSerializer._serialize_path`).

`Field.deconstruct` returns the field's name first, which `ModelFieldSerializer` leaves out, and shortens the path of a class under `django.db.models.fields` to `django.db.models` (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.deconstruct`; [A field: the base class](../models/fields.md)).

`Q.deconstruct`, `Index.deconstruct` and `BaseConstraint.deconstruct` are written by hand, and each shortens its own module to `django.db.models` (`django/db/models/query_utils.py:Q.deconstruct`; [Constraints and indexes](../models/constraints.md)).
Other classes get the method from the decorator `deconstructible` (`django/utils/deconstruct.py:deconstructible`).

`Expression` is decorated, as is every validator class of `django/core/validators.py`; `F`, `Func`, `Value` and some others are decorated with a path in `django.db.models`, which is why a file has `models.F` and not `django.db.models.expressions.F` (`django/db/models/expressions.py:F`).

`Expression` is decorated, as is every validator class of `django/core/validators.py`; `F`, `Func`, `Value` and some others are decorated with a path in `django.db.models`, which is why a file has `models.F` and not `django.db.models.expressions.F` (`django/db/models/expressions.py:F`).
`FunctionTypeSerializer` takes what `FUNCTION_TYPES` lists, functions, built-in functions and methods among them (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:FunctionTypeSerializer`).
Anything else is written as its `__module__` and `__qualname__` (`django/utils/module_loading.py:qualname`): a function at the top of a module, or in the body of a class.

`TypeSerializer` writes a class by module and qualified name too, except `models.Model` and `types.NoneType`, written under those names, and a builtin, written bare with no import (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:TypeSerializer`).
A **`SettingsReference`** is a `str` that also holds a setting's name, in `SettingsReference.setting_name` (`django/conf/__init__.py:SettingsReference`).

A field makes one: where `RelatedField.swappable_setting` names a setting, as it does for a field that points at the user model, which `AUTH_USER_MODEL` can swap, `ForeignObject.deconstruct` and `ManyToManyField.deconstruct` put a `SettingsReference` in place of the `"to"` argument (`django/db/models/fields/related.py:ForeignObject.deconstruct`).

`RegexSerializer` writes a pattern's flags after an exclusive-or with those of an empty `str` pattern, and none where that leaves none: `'^m-'` compiled with `re.IGNORECASE` is written `re.compile('^m-', 2)`, without the `re.UNICODE` that Python added (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:RegexSerializer`).

For a list, a tuple or a set, `BaseSequenceSerializer.serialize` writes each item and joins the strings, and a subclass gives the brackets through `BaseSequenceSerializer._format`: a tuple of one item gets its comma, and an empty set is `set()`, since `{}` is a dictionary (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:BaseSequenceSerializer`).
The entries of `Serializer._registry` stand in the order `serializer_factory` tries them, so a row takes only what no row above it took (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:Serializer`).

A function is written by name, and a lambda has none to import by: `FunctionTypeSerializer` refuses it, a function with no module, and one for which `qualname` raises, as it does for a function defined inside another, whose qualified name has `"<"` in it (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:FunctionTypeSerializer.serialize`).

`Serializer.register` takes a type, or a tuple of types, and a serializer class; it raises `ValueError` for a class that is no subclass of `BaseSerializer` and otherwise stores the pair, and `Serializer.unregister` pops a key; `MigrationWriter.register_serializer` and `MigrationWriter.unregister_serializer` only call the two (`django/db/migrations/serializer.py:Serializer.register`).
